newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hopewell's CEPA sale boosts outlook.
newsitem.headline: Hopewell's CEPA sale boosts outlook.

text.p: The planned sale by Hopewell Holdings Ltd of a large portion of its holding in subsidiary Consolidated Electric Power Asia Ltd (CEPA) generated some praise from often bearish analysts.

"The sale of CEPA shares at an 80 percent premium to book value (as carried by Hopewell in its accounts) augurs well for future projects including the sale of a stake in BERTS," said one analyst, who is recommending a buy for Hopewell.
BERTS is the Bangkok Elevated Rail and Transport System for which Hopewell holds a 30-year concession to build and operate.
Analysts expect a Thai partner to take up an interest in the project within the next year or so.
Despite the cash injection from the sale of CEPA shares, many analysts said they were wary about corporate earnings.
Hopewell chairman Gordon Wu said on Thursday Hopewell's gearing was 92 percent and would fall to as low as 23 percent as a result of the deal.
Analysts said Hopewell's high gearing creates high interest expense which drains cash flow and reduces working capital for other projects.
"Cash flow will be better but still insufficient to support their cash needs," said Wendy Ko, director of Hong Kong and China research at W.I. Carr.
Hopewell's results for the year ended June 30, 1996 showed an attributable profit of HK$769.19 million, compared with HK$2.1 billion for the previous year.
Despite mid-year warnings on delayed projects in the Philippines and China in 1996, the results were below expectations.
"Turnover rose while profits declined, pointing to a surge in interest expense," Ko said.
The results included an exceptional item of HK$223.89 million, whereas the 1995 results included a gain of HK$1.53 billion. CEPA contributed the 1996 exceptional gain from power station development.
CEPA announced an attributable profit of HK$637.79 million, a 12.9 percent increase over the previous year. These results were also below expectations, analysts said.
As a result, CEPA contributed HK$385 million to Hopewell's 1996 earnings, or 50 percent of total net earnings, said one analyst.
If the proposed sale of 80 percent of Hopewell's 60.4 percent-holding in CEPA to Southern Co is completed, Hopewell will receive a total of HK$9.7 billion before expenses, said the analyst.

"The sale enables Hopewell to realise an 80 percent appreciation on its CEPA assets and significantly reduce its borrowings and interest expense or reap more than sufficient interest income to offset the loss of CEPA earnings. Analysts who are positive on the stock cite attractive price to book ratios in relation to similar plays.
"Other listed infrastructure plays are trading at large premiums to their book value, yet Hopewell is trading at a big discount to its book value," said the analyst.
However, in its results announcement the company stated that its net tangible asset value as at end June 30, 1996 was HK$5.35 per share.
The share, which closed HK$4.95 on Friday, is trading at a 7.5 percent discount to its 1996 book value.
-- Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843-6352
